text: dsh-tool-guardian 是面向 DSH 的工具路由插件，接入原生工具注册表并通过 Python bridge 连接已有 MCP servers。它按需发现工具、展示能力和分组成本，再把选中的调用转发给后端；也可把工具结果压缩并归档较长原文，支持运行时激活工具组、恢复上次会话使用的组，以及检测 shell 绕过路由。适合连接多个 MCP 服务并控制工具定义占用上下文的 DSH 用户。需要本机 Python 和 MCP server 配置，不要求额外 API key。

dsh-tool-guardian routes MCP servers through native DSH tools and a Python bridge. It discovers capabilities on demand, forwards calls, shapes long results, and lets users activate or restore tool groups. It suits DSH users who want several MCP services without loading every schema at once.
我想把多个 MCP 服务接到 DSH，但不想每次都加载全部工具定义。
有没有办法先查看可用工具，再按任务加载其中一组？
让 DSH 把工具调用转给现有 MCP server。
工具返回内容太长，怎样压缩后再交给模型看？
我想在会话里临时启用某个 MCP 工具组。
换了会话后，能不能找回上次启用的工具组？
I want to route several MCP servers through a small set of DSH tools.
Can I load only the tool group needed for the current task?
dsh-tool-guardian 的功能「工具路由」：通过 DSH 原生工具列出后端能力并转发指定 server/tool 调用。先发现工具，再提交参数并取得后端结果。
dsh-tool-guardian 的功能「结果整理」：工具结果可按类型清理、压缩或采样，较长原文可归档供后续取回。该处理在结果交给模型前触发。
dsh-tool-guardian 的功能「按组加载」：用户可查看工具组及成本，并在会话中激活所需组；组内工具随后作为 DSH 原生工具注册。
dsh-tool-guardian 的功能「会话命令」：/toolguardian 命令提供自检、绕过情况查看和恢复上次工具组等操作。命令由 DSH command registry 注册。

dsh-tool-guardian README · When *not* to use the router：- **Your client already searches tools for you.** Some clients (and some model APIs) load tool
  definitions on demand themselves. Putting a router under that adds a hop and a second catalogue
  for no saving.
- **You run a handful of small servers.** The router's own tools cost about 1,100 tokens of
  `tools/list`; one small server behind it is close to break-even (`--selftest` prints the real
  arithmetic for *your* servers before you commit to it). The saving grows with every server added
  and is largest where it matters most — a 32K local model with half a dozen servers.

text:
dsh-tool-guardian README · Why this exists：MCP tool definitions are re-sent on **every single request**, whether the model touches them or not. A handful of servers routinely comes to tens of thousands of tokens — often most of a small local model's window — before the first user message. On one real setup, seven MCP servers came to **28,689 tokens, 87.6% of a 32K window**, as a fixed floor under everything else.

You have two ways to deal with that today, and both cost you something:

dsh-tool-guardian README · Why this exists：| Approach | The cost |
|---|---|
| Load fewer MCP servers | You lose the capability entirely |
| Live with it | Two-thirds of the window is gone before you type |

Tool Guardian is a third option that costs neither. It fronts all your servers and shows the model just a handful of small tools plus a one-line catalogue of server names (1,084 tokens with seven servers behind it, measured below). The full schema for a tool is fetched only when the model asks for it:

dsh-tool-guardian README · Why this exists：```
list_capabilities(server?)      one line per tool — names and purpose
describe_tool(server, tool)     the full argument schema for ONE tool
call_tool(server, tool, args)   invoke it, return the result
```

Same idea as a search index: cheap catalogue always visible, detail on demand.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Why this exists：Every tool carries the MCP annotations (`title`, `readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`, `idempotentHint`, `openWorldHint`). All of them are read-only except `call_tool`, which is marked destructive and open-world because it runs whatever the backend tool does; the DSH bundle's `tg__*` direct tools carry the same values.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Model requirement (read this before you switch)：The whole design rests on one behaviour: the model must **proactively call `list_capabilities` (then `call_tool`) when it needs a tool.** Capable/frontier models do this reliably. Small local models are less certain — and, as the two measurements below show, **the harness the model runs in matters as much as the model.**
section: Model requirement (read this before you switch)

text: dsh-tool-guardian README · Model requirement (read this before you switch)：**Measurement 1 — August 2026, OpenClaude, router mounted over MCP.** Against a real multi-server stack, **gpt-oss:20b and qwen3-30b-a3b both bypassed the router** on ordinary tasks — even with the `NEXT STEP` nudge in every result *and* a dedicated router sub-agent priming them. They treated a tool name as a shell command or scripted their way around it. Part of that was the harness, not the models: gpt-oss:20b did call `list_capabilities` correctly but could not carry the discovery into `call_tool` inside a general task, and the one approach that completed the sequence (the sub-agent) was blocked by the harness's own agent-tool argument validation before it ever reached the router.

text: dsh-tool-guardian README · Model requirement (read this before you switch)：So: `--selftest` proves the *saving* and that your backends start — it does **not** prove your model will drive the router in your harness. **Test discovery→call with your actual model and harness before committing**, and measure rather than guess: every router call is appended to `~/.tool-guardian/calls.jsonl` (`TOOL_GUARDIAN_CALL_LOG`) with a session id, and under DSH a shell call that does a router tool's job is logged there as `kind: "bypass"` (and can be nudged or denied). After a few real tasks, **`/toolguardian bypass`** (DSH) or **`tool-guardian --bypass-summary`** (any client) reads that file for you: router calls, every bypass with the exact `call_tool(...)` it should have been, and sessions that never touched the router. Over plain MCP, see [bypass detection and its limits](#bypass-detection-over-plain-mcp-and-its-limits). If it won't, expose a small *curated, visible* subset of servers instead of routing everything behind a catalogue the model never opens.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Tools：The router exposes these tools. The first four are always there; `list_groups_with_costs` and `retrieve_spill` (while the output ladder is on) are the other two of the 6 router tools; the two skill tools appear only when a skill folder is configured.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Tools：| tool | arguments | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `list_capabilities` | `server` (optional) | tool names with one-line summaries for one server, or all; start here |
| `search_capabilities` | `query`, `server` and `limit` (optional) | find a tool by keyword across servers |
| `describe_tool` | `server`, `tool`, `detail` (optional) | the arguments of one tool (`detail=full`: its whole schema) |
| `call_tool` | `server`, `tool`, `args` (optional) | run a backend tool and return its (shaped) result; this is the step that answers the user |
| `list_groups_with_costs` | none | tool groups and the context-token cost of loading each |
| `retrieve_spill` | `id`, `grep`, `start_line`, `max_lines` (optional) | read back the full original of a shortened result |
| `list_skills` | none | one line per skill (only with `TOOL_GUARDIAN_SKILLS`) |
| `read_skill` | `name` | the full text of one skill (only with `TOOL_GUARDIAN_SKILLS`) |

dsh-tool-guardian README · Tools：All but `call_tool` only report (read-only, no network: the catalogue is in memory, the archive and skills on local disk); `call_tool` does whatever the backend tool does. Each tool's description says what it is for, when a sibling is the better call, what it touches and what comes back — in about one clause each, because the whole `tools/list` payload is capped at 1,100 tokens by a test. Every parameter is typed and explained exactly once, by its own description, by its `enum`, or by the tool description naming it; `tests/test_tool_definitions.py` checks that, and checks this table's argument names against the schemas the server really lists.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Search by meaning (optional)：`search_capabilities` matches words. Ask it to "persist a memo" and it finds nothing, because no tool says "persist" or "memo"; the tool is `add_note`. Search by meaning fixes that with an embedding model you run yourself. **It is off by default**: with `TOOL_GUARDIAN_EMBED_URL` unset the output is byte for byte what it was and nothing is sent anywhere.

Turn it on by pointing it at an embeddings endpoint. The URL path tells tool-guardian which shape to speak:

```bash
dsh-tool-guardian README · Ollama (the path ends in /api/embed)：export TOOL_GUARDIAN_EMBED_URL=http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/embed

dsh-tool-guardian README · or any OpenAI-compatible server (the path ends in /embeddings)：export TOOL_GUARDIAN_EMBED_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/embeddings
```

| variable | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `TOOL_GUARDIAN_EMBED_URL` | unset (off) | the embeddings endpoint; a path that ends in neither `/api/embed` nor `/embeddings` is refused and search stays on keywords |
nomic-embed-text   recall@3 keyword=35.0 semantic=80.0 blended=80.0 over 40 queries
mxbai-embed-large  recall@3 keyword=35.0 semantic=85.0 blended=82.5 over 40 queries
```

dsh-tool-guardian README · or any OpenAI-compatible server (the path ends in /embeddings)：Run it on your own model: `python bench/bench_search.py --url http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/embed --model <name> --min 0.5`.

Why meaning first: a blend that let keywords outweigh meaning scored only 45 to 47.5 on real embeddings, because a substring hit ("store" inside "storemanager") lists tools for unrelated queries and ranks them above the paraphrase match. So a keyword hit alone lists nothing, and keywords only order tools that already passed on meaning.

(Claude Code, Claude Desktop, ...)"] -- "stdio JSON-RPC" --> serve dsh["DSH bundle

tg_bridge.py" --> router subgraph tg["tool-guardian (Python, standard library only)"]

dsh-tool-guardian README · Architecture：You point your client at **one** MCP server, Tool Guardian, and give it the same `mcpServers` config you would have
given the client. It starts every backend as a child process at launch, reads each `tools/list` once, and from then on
answers `list_capabilities`, `search_capabilities` and `describe_tool` from memory. Only `call_tool` reaches a backend.
Its arguments are checked against the backend tool's schema first, and the result goes through the output ladder before
the model sees it. The DSH bundle reaches the same `Router` through a private bridge process instead of MCP.
dsh-tool-guardian README · Architecture：Key decisions, each with its trade-off (full records in [docs/adr/](docs/adr/)):

dsh-tool-guardian README · Architecture：| Decision | What it buys | What it costs |
|---|---|---|
| Generic router tools, schemas on demand ([0001](docs/adr/0001-router-with-on-demand-discovery.md)) | 91 % fewer schema tokens on every request (bench) | every capability is 2–3 calls away; the model must choose to look |
| Loud failure, named catalogue ([0002](docs/adr/0002-loud-failure-and-a-named-catalogue.md)) | a dead server is never mistaken for "no such tool" | the description grows a few tokens per server |
| Descriptions budgeted and pinned ([0003](docs/adr/0003-descriptions-are-paid-on-every-request.md)) | tools a model can choose between without guessing | 1,090 tokens of `tools/list` with no backends, pinned at ≤ 1,100 by a test |
| Lenient inputs, strict backend checks ([0004](docs/adr/0004-lenient-inputs-strict-checks.md)) | small models' near-miss calls still work; impossible calls cost no round trip | schemas are looser than what the router enforces |
| One stdlib Python core; DSH bundle is a bridge ([0005](docs/adr/0005-one-python-core-stdlib-only.md)) | installs anywhere; one router to fix | MCP stdio is hand-written; the npm package needs a Python |
| Archive before

dsh-tool-guardian README · Install：```bash
pip install tool-guardian
```

Pure standard library — nothing else to install.

> PyPI and npm now ship the same code: `pip install tool-guardian` (0.3.0+) for the MCP server, `dsh-tool-guardian` on npm for DSH.

Which install is which: the Python package `tool-guardian` **0.10.0** is the MCP server (`pip install tool-guardian`, or `uvx tool-guardian`); the npm package `dsh-tool-guardian` **0.10.0-beta.1** is the DeepSeek Harness bundle. They are versioned separately.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Configure：**Quickest way:** you probably already have your servers set up in another MCP client.

```bash
tool-guardian-setup import    # copies them from Claude Desktop / Cursor / Windsurf / .mcp.json, asks before writing
tool-guardian-setup doctor    # checks the config, each server's command, your .env and ${VARS}, and says how to fix each problem
```

**Adding one more server is one command** -- everything after `--` is the server's command line, exactly as you would type it:

dsh-tool-guardian README · Configure：```bash
tool-guardian-setup add git -- uvx mcp-server-git
tool-guardian-setup add github --env GITHUB_TOKEN='${GITHUB_TOKEN}' --description "issues and PRs" -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-github
tool-guardian-setup list      # name, command, and the group each server's tools land in
tool-guardian-setup remove git

dsh-tool-guardian README · Configure：`add` writes to the same config `doctor` finds (under DSH that is `$TOOL_GUARDIAN_CONFIG`), backs it up first, refuses a
name that already exists unless you pass `--replace`, checks the command is on your PATH, warns about any `${VAR}` that is
not set in your environment or `.env`, and ends with the doctor result for that one server. Then restart your MCP client
(or start a new DSH session) to load it.
Every server you add is automatically behind the router's 6 tools: with no groups config it gets its own group named
after the server; with a custom groups config it lands in `other` until you add it to a group.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Configure：`import` writes `~/.tool-guardian/mcp.json` (backing up any existing file) and skips `"url"` servers (it does not
copy them yet; add one to `~/.tool-guardian/mcp.json` by hand, see [Remote servers](#remote-servers)). For each
skipped server it prints the one entry to put in your client instead. Inside DSH (npm install) run the
same thing as `python <plugin folder>/tg_setup.py doctor`.

Or write the config by hand:

dsh-tool-guardian README · Configure：Config is searched in order: `--config PATH`, `$TOOL_GUARDIAN_CONFIG`, `~/.tool-guardian/mcp.json`. Whichever file is used is printed to stderr at startup, with the `.env` that was loaded beside it.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Configure：**A config in the current directory needs your say-so.** `./mcp.json` and `./.mcp.json` are *not* loaded automatically. A repository you cloned can carry one, and up to 0.7.0 starting the router inside that directory launched its servers — with no approval prompt from your client. When one is found and skipped you get a single stderr line naming it and the opt-in; to use it, pass `--config ./mcp.json`, set `TOOL_GUARDIAN_CONFIG=./mcp.json`, or set `TOOL_GUARDIAN_PROJECT_CONFIG=1`.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Configure：A `./.mcp.json` whose only server is tool-guardian itself (what the Claude Code setup below writes, to register the router with the client) is never treated as the router's own config: it is skipped and the search carries on to `~/.tool-guardian/mcp.json`.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Environment and `.env`：Tool Guardian loads a `.env` itself and expands variables in your backend
args, so secrets don't have to be exported into the environment by whatever
launches it.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Environment and `.env`：- **`.env` autoload.** On startup it looks for a `.env` in this order: an
  explicit path, `$TOOL_GUARDIAN_ENV`, then an **upward search** — starting at
  the config file's directory (or the cwd) and walking up to 5 parent
  directories, loading the first `.env` it finds. This lets your config live
  in a nested folder while the `.env` sits at the project root. Values already
  in the real environment win over the file, and the `TOOL_GUARDIAN_*` settings
  themselves can live there too; a missing `.env` is a no-op,
  never an error.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Environment and `.env`：Example — config nested under the project, `.env` at the root:

myproject/
      ├── .env                 <- (3) found here, loaded, search stops
      └── config/
          └── dsh/
              └── mcp.json      <- $TOOL_GUARDIAN_CONFIG points here

The search walks upward from the config's directory:

1. myproject/config/dsh/.env    -> not found
      2. myproject/config/.env        -> not found
      3. myproject/.env               -> FOUND  (stops here)

dsh-tool-guardian README · Environment and `.env`：- **Small-window preset.** `TOOL_GUARDIAN_PRESET=small` is for 8k-context local
  models. It sets exactly two values:

dsh-tool-guardian README · Environment and `.env`：| setting | default | `small` | what it does |
  |---|--:|--:|---|
  | `TOOL_GUARDIAN_CATALOGUE_CHARS` | 0 (no cap) | 1500 | each server's block in `list_capabilities` is cut at this many characters, with a `[+N more tools not shown ...]` line pointing at `search_capabilities` |
  | `TOOL_GUARDIAN_DESC_WORDS` | 12 | 6 | words of a tool, server or skill description shown in catalogue and search lines |

dsh-tool-guardian README · Environment and `.env`：`small` also turns on `TOOL_GUARDIAN_TERSE` (below). Set either variable to override the preset. Search ranking still scores 12
  description words, the output ladder and every other setting are unchanged, and
  `describe_tool` is compact in both. On the seven bench catalogues the seven
  per-server listings total 9,582 characters with `small` against 16,274 without.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Environment and `.env`：- **Terse router tools.** `TOOL_GUARDIAN_TERSE=1` serves the router's own tools with one-sentence
  descriptions (at most 160 characters), no per-parameter descriptions, and without
  `list_groups_with_costs`. Names, argument types, enums, defaults, required arguments and the MCP
  annotation hints are unchanged, and `list_capabilities` still names the live servers. `tools/list`
  drops from 1,090 to about 617 tokens. It is on under `TOOL_GUARDIAN_PRESET=small` unless you set
  `TOOL_GUARDIAN_TERSE=0`; unset or `0` leaves the default payload exactly as it was.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Environment and `.env`：- **Variable expansion.** `${VAR}`, `$VAR` and `%VAR%` are expanded in each
  backend's `args` **and in its `env` values** from the environment; unknown
  variables are left as-is, so the backend's own error names the one you missed.
  Keep a secret in `.env` and reference it in a backend arg:

"args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://app.openseo.so/mcp",
               "--header", "Authorization: Bearer ${OPENSEO_API_KEY}"]

or in a backend's environment:

dsh-tool-guardian README · Remote servers：- `headers` values take `${VAR}` exactly as `env` does (from the environment or `.env`). `type` may be `"http"` or
  `"streamable-http"`, or left out; `"sse"` forces the older HTTP+SSE transport (below).
- `https://` always verifies the certificate. `http://` is allowed to `127.0.0.1`, `localhost` and `::1` only; any other
  host fails with `plaintext http to a non-loopback host; set allowInsecure true for this server`. Add
  `"allowInsecure": true` to that server's entry to accept it.
- `HTTPS_PROXY` / `HTTP_PROXY` are honoured (HTTPS goes through a `CONNECT` tunnel) and so is `NO_PROXY`.
- The router asks each server which revision it speaks, once, when it starts: the stateless **2026-07-28** revision
  (`server/discover`), else the stateful **2025-11-25**, **2025-06-18** or **2025-03-26** (`initialize`, with a session
  id if the server issues one, ended with `DELETE` when the router stops). `tool-guardian --selftest` prints one line
  per remote server that is up:

dsh-tool-guardian README · Remote servers：- **HTTP+SSE (2024-11-05) is spoken too.** Old servers still exist, and the transport is **Deprecated** upstream
  (it is still allowed for a twelve-month window), so the router speaks it rather than leave them out. Set
  `"type": "sse"` and the router opens one `GET` stream, takes the `endpoint` event as the URL to `POST` to
  (a path is resolved against the server's origin; an endpoint on another origin is refused), and reads every reply
  from the stream. Without a `type`, the router falls back to it, once and in this order, when `server/discover` and
  then `initialize` are both refused with 400, 404 or 405 and a `GET` answers with an `endpoint` event. `headers`
  go on the `GET` and on every `POST`. If the stream closes, or the endpoint answers 404, the router reconnects once
  (a new `GET`, a new `initialize`) and re-sends the request with a new id; a second failure is reported as for any
  other server. Closing sends no `DELETE`. `--selftest` prints `[remote] <name>: sse 2024-11-05 <n> tools`.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Remote servers：Failures take the path a stdio server does: one reconnect after a short wait (a legacy server's session is
re-initialized), then `DOWN` on a second failure within a minute. A `401` shows the server as `AUTH_REQUIRED` with its
`WWW-Authenticate` header, which carries the `resource_metadata` URL.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Run：```bash
claude mcp add --scope user tool-guardian -- tool-guardian --config /path/to/your/mcp.json
```

In a container: `docker build -t tool-guardian .` then `docker run -i --rm -v "$HOME/.tool-guardian:/root/.tool-guardian" tool-guardian`.
The backends run inside the container too, so the image needs whatever they are started with (`npx`, `uvx`, ...); the
bundled [`Dockerfile`](Dockerfile) has Python only.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Run：Everything your servers can do is still reachable — the model just discovers it in two steps (`list_capabilities` → `call_tool`) instead of paying for all of it up front.

dsh-tool-guardian README · A backend that exits or stops answering：When a backend's process exits, or a call gets no reply within `TOOL_GUARDIAN_CALL_TIMEOUT`, the router stops it and
starts it again before the next call: after 1 s the first time, 5 s on any later respawn, re-sending the `initialize`
handshake. A second failure within 60 s marks the backend `DOWN` and it is not restarted again. The count is
`backend_respawns` in the bridge's `stats` and the `backend respawns: N since load` line of `/toolguardian`.

text: dsh-tool-guardian README · See what it saves：Starts your configured servers, prints the catalogue, and reports the tokens the router tools cost versus loading every server's tools directly — e.g. with one filesystem server behind it: *"router tools cost ~840 tokens vs ~3943 for the full set behind them -> ~3103 tokens freed on every request (79% smaller)"*. One small server is close to break-even; the saving grows with every server added. Below the totals it prints one `[server] N tools, ~M tokens` line per server, and it exits non-zero if any configured server failed to start. It ends with one `update:` line (a newer release, "none", or "could not check"); `tool-guardian-setup doctor` ends with the same line. dsh-tool-guardian README · Count what it saved in real use：- **Catalogue tokens avoided** is the number of sessions started in the window × (what every live server's `tools/list` costs − what the router's own costs). Both costs are written to `state.json` each time the router starts, so a log from before 0.8.3 prints `unknown` until the router has started once. TOOL_GUARDIAN_PROVE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 tool-guardian --prove

text: dsh-tool-guardian README · Prove your model drives the router：Sends three bundled prompts to an OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint with the router tools attached, runs the model's tool calls through a real router in front of a bundled stub server, and prints one `PASS`/`FAIL` line per prompt with the prompt and completion tokens the endpoint reported: `list_describe` (list or search, then `describe_tool`), `nested_call` (`call_tool` with a nested filter), `stalled` (the model must reach `call_tool`, not only search). Exit 0 when all pass, 1 on any `FAIL`, 2 when `TOOL_GUARDIAN_PROVE_URL` is not set. Optional: `TOOL_GUARDIAN_PROVE_MODEL` (default: the first id from `GET <url>/models`), `TOOL_GUARDIAN_PROVE_KEY` (bearer token). The servers in your `mcp.json` are not started, and nothing is written to the call log or `state.json`. Your tool policy file is ignored (it prints `prove: policy off`): this is a capability test on the bundled stub server, and a `deny` or `readOnly` rule would fail it for the wrong reason.

text: dsh-tool-guardian README · It keeps tool *results* small too (0.3.0)：Definitions are half the problem; one 40 KB build log is the other half. Every `call_tool` result now goes down a deterministic **output ladder** before the model sees it:

dsh-tool-guardian README · It keeps tool *results* small too (0.3.0)：| result | what the model gets |
|---|---|
| under ~1.2k chars, or from a `read`-class tool | untouched, byte for byte |
| an error over 300 chars | head + tail summary |
| JSON array / CSV ≥ 10k | keys, first and last items, counts |
| shell-style output ≥ 8k | head, evenly spaced samples (with line numbers), tail — `[exit code: …]` always kept |
| a unified diff | every change, plus the context right next to it |
| anything else ≥ 1.2k | cleaned losslessly: ANSI stripped, blank runs collapsed, repeated lines counted |

dsh-tool-guardian README · It keeps tool *results* small too (0.3.0)：**Nothing is lost silently.** Before any lossy step the full original is archived, the result says so in one line, and the model can call **`retrieve_spill(id, grep=…)`** to read it back. If the archive cannot be written, the original is returned instead. Same input, same output, always — so provider prompt caches keep hitting. `TOOL_GUARDIAN_LADDER=0` turns it off.

dsh-tool-guardian README · It keeps tool *results* small too (0.3.0)：`list_groups_with_costs` prices each tool group in context tokens, and every router call is logged (argument *values* never are) to `~/.tool-guardian/calls.jsonl` so you can measure whether your model actually uses the router.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Skills：The same catalogue-on-demand idea, applied to `SKILL.md` files. Point `TOOL_GUARDIAN_SKILLS` at one or more folders (separated by `:` on Linux/macOS, `;` on Windows); every `SKILL.md` one or two levels below a root is a skill, named by its front-matter `name` (or its folder).

dsh-tool-guardian README · Skills：- **`list_skills`** — one line per skill: name and purpose. Its description names every skill, so the model knows they exist.
- **`read_skill(name)`** — the full text of one skill. A name is a name, never a path: `/`, `\` and `..` are refused.

The two tools appear only when at least one skill is found. `tool-guardian --skills-report` prints what the catalogue saves against loading every skill up front.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Measured savings：Reproduce it yourself: `python bench/bench_tokens.py` (no network, no model; `--json` for machine output). The catalogs are the real `tools/list` answers of seven public MCP servers, recorded in `bench/fixtures/catalogs/`.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Measured savings：| server | tools | tokens of tool schemas |
|---|--:|--:|
| everything | 13 | 1,610 |
| filesystem | 14 | 2,500 |
| github | 26 | 5,094 |
| memory | 9 | 1,347 |
| n8n-mcp | 7 | 2,826 |
| playwright | 25 | 5,443 |
| sequential-thinking | 1 | 1,185 |
| **all seven** | **95** | **20,005** |

dsh-tool-guardian README · Measured savings：**Every request:** 20,005 tokens of tool schemas without tool-guardian, 1,084 with it (**94.6 % less**). On a 32K-context local model that is the difference between a window that is 61 % full before the conversation starts and one that is 3 % full. (The 2026-10-21 description rewrite had pushed this to 1,790; [ADR 0003](docs/adr/0003-descriptions-are-paid-on-every-request.md) records the budget that brought it back.)

The output ladder on four typical tool results:

dsh-tool-guardian README · Measured savings：| output | tool | before (chars) | after (chars) | how |
|---|---|--:|--:|---|
| 3,000-line build log with one error | bash | 115,945 | 4,540 | head, samples, the error line, tail, exit code |
| 400-item JSON array | http_get | 29,521 | 730 | keys, first and last items, counts |
| 3-hunk unified diff | git_diff | 41,764 | 1,363 | every change plus 2 lines of context |
| 1,500-row CSV | query | 44,882 | 354 | header, first and last rows, counts |

dsh-tool-guardian README · Measured savings：Every shortened result is archived first and can be read back with `retrieve_spill`. Token counts use `tiktoken` (cl100k) when it is installed and a conservative characters ÷ 3.5 estimate otherwise; the table above is the estimate.

dsh-tool-guardian README · What it costs per task (measured 2026-10-01)：The saving above is **per request**. A tool behind the router has to be found before it can be called, and every extra
model request re-sends the conversation, so what matters for a whole task is *requests per task*. Measured on a real
DeepSeek Harness setup -- qwen3-coder:30b (Ollama, 64K window), 3 servers / 26 tools, 8 read-only tasks x 2 repeats, one
fresh session per task, the same tasks with the servers mounted directly vs. behind tool-guardian:

dsh-tool-guardian README · What it costs per task (measured 2026-10-01)：| | direct mount | tool-guardian 0.4.0 | tool-guardian 0.4.1 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| tools in the request header | 64 | 33 | 33 |
| header tokens per request | 17,831 | 10,825 | 10,825 |
| model requests per task | 1.9 | 4.8 | **2.8** |
| est. input tokens per task | 39,692 | 73,609 | **38,089** |
| wall time per task | 41 s | 75 s | 44 s |
| tasks passed (of 16) | 6 | 8 | 7 |

dsh-tool-guardian README · What it costs per task (measured 2026-10-01)：0.4.0 cut every request by 39 % but cost 85 % more per task: the model went search -> describe -> call, and copied the
call-shaped `NEXT STEP` hints as plain text. 0.4.1 puts each hit's arguments into the search result (no describe round
trip) and drops call syntax from the hints; per-task cost is now about even with a direct mount on 3 servers, and the
saving grows with every server you add. Break-even on this setup is ~3.7 requests per task. Pass rates at n = 16 are
inside noise. **When it pays off:** many servers, long sessions, a model that goes search -> call. **When it does not:**
one or two small servers with a model that explores. Reproduce: the harness and raw scores are in the 2026-10-01 entry of
the CHANGELOG.

dsh-tool-guardian README · It catches the mistakes small models make (0.4.0)：Local models get tool calls *almost* right: a count sent as `"2"`, a required argument left out, a made-up option, the
same failing call repeated until the context runs out. The router now sits in front of those mistakes:
section: It catches the mistakes small models make (0.4.0)

text:
dsh-tool-guardian README · It catches the mistakes small models make (0.4.0)：| mistake | what happens |
|---|---|
| a quoted number, `"true"`/`"false"`, a number where text is expected | fixed silently, then sent |
| a required argument missing, a wrong type, a value outside the allowed list, an unknown key on a closed schema | **not sent**; the model gets each problem and a correct example call |
| the same call returning the same result a 3rd time | the result is prefixed with a one-line "repeating this will not change the answer" |
| the same call a 5th time | not run; the model is told to use what it has or say what is blocking it |
section: It catches the mistakes small models make (0.4.0)

text:
dsh-tool-guardian README · It catches the mistakes small models make (0.4.0)：Finding a tool is cheaper too: `search_capabilities(query)` returns the few matching `server.tool: description`
lines instead of a whole catalogue. Switches: `TG_VALIDATE_ARGS=0`, `TG_LOOP_GUARD=0`.
section: It catches the mistakes small models make (0.4.0)

text:
dsh-tool-guardian README · Nested arguments：The checks above walk nested objects and array items too (required keys, types, enum values, closed objects), and a
problem names its full path: `argument 'params.filters[2].op' must be one of: eq, lt, gt`.

dsh-tool-guardian README · `describe_tool` detail：`describe_tool(server, tool)` returns the compact form by default: `server.tool: one-line description`, a
`required args:` line, and the NEXT STEP line listing every argument (`?` = optional). `detail="full"` returns the
whole tool definition as before. On the seven bench catalogues (95 tools) compact is 25,161 characters against
131,080 for full, 80.8 % shorter. `TOOL_GUARDIAN_DESCRIBE_DETAIL=full` makes full the default.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Native DeepSeek Harness (DSH) bundle：The same repo is an installable DSH bundle, `dsh-tool-guardian`. The Python router is unchanged — the bundle is a bridge to it, not a rewrite, and the MCP server above keeps working.

```sh
dsh plugin --profile <name> add dsh-tool-guardian        # or a path to a checkout (run `pnpm install` in it first)
dsh --profile <name> --dump-config                        # shows a "# == dsh-tool-guardian" layer
```

dsh-tool-guardian README · Native DeepSeek Harness (DSH) bundle：Inside DSH it (1) registers the router tools **natively**, so your MCP backends' schemas never enter a request unless you activate their group (`activeGroups`, or the `activate_group` tool, which quotes the token cost first); (2) runs the output ladder on **every** tool's result — `bash`, `grep`, `web_fetch`, all of them — through `tools/post-execute`, so do not mount `dsh-trim` beside it; (3) notices shell calls that do a router tool's job and logs, nudges (default) or denies them (`bypass.mode`). Configure it in the profile's `cordis.patch.yml` by overriding the `tool-guardian` row, or through the DSH settings namespace `tool-guardian`; the existing `TOOL_GUARDIAN_*` environment variables win over both. Python is found at `$TOOL_GUARDIAN_PYTHON`, then a `.venv` beside the package, then `python`/`python3` on `PATH` (3.9+, standard library only).

dsh-tool-guardian README · Native DeepSeek Harness (DSH) bundle：**Setup and checks.** `npm run setup` in the plugin folder finds Python, imports the MCP servers you already use into `~/.tool-guardian/mcp.json` (asking first) and runs the doctor; the bridge finds that file by itself, so no preset or YAML is edited. In a session, `/toolguardian` is the selftest, `/toolguardian bypass` (or `bypass last`, `bypass 24h`) the bypass summary, and `/toolguardian restore` re-loads the previous session's groups.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Native DeepSeek Harness (DSH) bundle：**Groups across sessions.** Each `activate_group` is remembered in `~/.tool-guardian/state.json` (`TOOL_GUARDIAN_STATE`; empty disables). The next session is *offered* those groups — a log line, a line in `list_groups_with_costs`, the `restore_groups` tool and `/toolguardian restore` — and never loads them on its own, because every loaded group costs tokens on every request.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Native DeepSeek Harness (DSH) bundle：**Settings.** There is no card for Tool Guardian in the DSH web UI (DSH draws cards only for plugins that ship a browser bundle); the settings live under `tool-guardian:` in `~/.dsh/settings.yaml` and apply live. [docs/dsh-settings.md](docs/dsh-settings.md) shows every field as a card and the exact precedence order, proven line by line from the code.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Native DeepSeek Harness (DSH) bundle：The result-shaping design follows [dsh-trim](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dsh-trim) (shuistama, MIT): `next()` first, fail open, archive before anything lossy.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Tool policy: deny, ask, read-only：`call_tool` runs whatever tool the model names. A policy file lets you block tools, make the model confirm others, or make a whole session read-only. It is `$TOOL_GUARDIAN_POLICY`, else `~/.tool-guardian/policy.json`, and it is read when the router starts (restart to change it):

```json
{"readOnly": false,
 "servers": {"*":     {"deny": ["^delete_"]},
             "files": {"allow": ["^read_", "^list_"], "ask": ["write|move"]}}}
```

dsh-tool-guardian README · Tool policy: deny, ask, read-only：- A server's own entry and `"*"` are merged. Each regex is `re.search`ed on the bare tool name (no `server.` prefix).
- Order: `readOnly`, then `deny`, then an `allow` list that nothing in it matches (that tool is denied, rule `allow`), then `ask`. Otherwise the tool is allowed. No file means no policy: the router behaves exactly as it did before.
- **A denied tool is invisible.** `list_capabilities`, `search_capabilities` and `list_groups_with_costs` leave it out, and `call_tool` (or `describe_tool`) on it returns `POLICY_DENIED <rule>` without calling the server.
- **A file that is not valid JSON, or has a bad regex, fails closed:** every `call_tool` returns `POLICY_DENIED policy file unreadable: ...` until you fix it.
- Every deny and every ask is written to the call log as a `kind: "policy"` row (server, tool name, decision, rule; never the arguments), and `tool-guardian --bypass-summary` adds a line `policy denials: <n>`.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Tool policy: deny, ask, read-only：Three examples:

```json
{"readOnly": true}
```

A read-only session: only tools whose server marks them `readOnlyHint: true` are visible or callable.

```json
{"servers": {"*": {"deny": ["^delete_"]}}}
```

Deny every `delete_...` tool on every server.

```json
{"servers": {"*": {"ask": ["shell|exec|write|rm"]}}}
```

Ask before anything whose name contains `shell`, `exec`, `write` or `rm`.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Tool policy: deny, ask, read-only：**`readOnly` trusts the server's own hints.** MCP tool annotations (`readOnlyHint` and friends) are written by the server and are untrusted: a server can mark a destructive tool read-only, and the router cannot tell. `readOnly` narrows what a well-behaved server exposes; it is not a sandbox. A server that sends no annotations has no tool marked `readOnlyHint: true`, so **`"readOnly": true` denies everything on it**: use `allow` for those servers.

dsh-tool-guardian README · What `ask` is: a token the model hands back：`call_tool` on an `ask` tool does not run it. It returns `CONFIRM_REQUIRED <token>` and one sentence on how to go ahead. The model then calls `call_tool` again with the same `server`, `tool` and `args` plus a top-level `confirm`:

```json
{"server": "files", "tool": "write_file", "args": {"path": "a.txt", "text": "hi"}, "confirm": "<token>"}
```
section: What `ask` is: a token the model hands back

text: dsh-tool-guardian README · What `ask` is: a token the model hands back：`confirm` is deliberately not in the `call_tool` schema (the descriptions, and the 1,100-token `tools/list`, stay as they are); the router accepts it anyway. The token is an HMAC-SHA256 over the server, tool, arguments and a nonce under a secret that lives only in the running process, is valid for 120 seconds (`TOOL_GUARDIAN_CONFIRM_TTL`) and works once, for exactly that call. A token for other arguments, another tool, an expired or a used one runs nothing and you get a fresh `CONFIRM_REQUIRED`.
section: What `ask` is: a token the model hands back

text: dsh-tool-guardian README · What `ask` is: a token the model hands back：**The model confirms, not you -- unless your client offers elicitation (see [Ask a human](#ask-a-human)).** The token goes to the model and the model passes it back, so `ask` stops a model that has not thought about what it is about to do, not one that is trying to get round it. If your client cannot show a dialog and you need a person in the loop, use `deny`.

text: dsh-tool-guardian README · Poisoned-tool warning：At start, every backend tool's description and input schema is checked against `tg_poison_patterns.json`: instructions aimed at the model, `<IMPORTANT>`-style blocks, invisible characters, credential paths and send-it-to-a-URL orders. A flagged tool keeps working; `list_capabilities` shows ` ⚠ flagged: <codes>` on its line, `describe_tool` adds a `flags:` line, and a `call_tool` result whose first 64 KB matches gets one header line, `flagged: <codes> (result unchanged)`. The result body is never edited. Descriptions are pinned trust-on-first-use in `pins.json` beside `state.json`: the first start after an install pins whatever is there, and a later change adds the flag `description.changed`.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Poisoned-tool warning：`ask` uses the same confirmation as an `ask` rule (a dialog where the client supports one, else the confirm token); `deny` blocks the call and names the codes. An unknown `action` is a policy error, so the policy fails closed.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Ask for only the part you need (opt-in)：With `TOOL_GUARDIAN_INTENT=1`, `call_tool` takes an optional `intent` (up to 200 characters). When a result is big enough to be archived, only the chunks that match the intent come back, each marked `[chunk i/N]`, followed by a `searchable terms:` line and the `retrieve_spill` id of the full original. Without `intent`, or for a small result, the reply is exactly what it was.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Ask a human：On a client that can show a yes/no dialog, an `ask` rule asks **you** instead of handing the model a token. The dialog reads `Tool Guardian policy asks before running <server>.<tool>. Allow it?` with the arguments as compact JSON (left out when they are longer than 200 characters). The tool runs only if you answer yes.

**Which clients get the dialog:**

dsh-tool-guardian README · Ask a human：- a client that negotiated protocol `2025-06-18` or `2025-11-25` in `initialize` **and** declared the `elicitation` capability in form mode (`{}` or `{"form": {}}`); or
- a `2026-07-28` request that carries form elicitation in its `_meta` client capabilities. That revision has no `initialize`, so the router answers the call with `resultType: "input_required"` and one elicitation request, and runs the tool when the retry comes back with your yes. The `requestState` it hands out is signed, works once and is tied to that server, tool and arguments.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Ask a human：**Tested with Claude Code** 2.1.302 on Windows (2026-10-31): the call opens a box headed `MCP server "<name>" requests your input` with the question above and a required **Run it** checkbox. Press Space to tick it, then choose Accept: the tool runs. Choose Decline: nothing runs and the model is told `USER_DECLINED decline`. Claude Code will not accept the form with the box unticked, so `unconfirmed` does not come up there. The call log showed one `"via": "elicitation"` row per question, and the model was never given a token.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Ask a human：**Every other client keeps the confirm token** described above: `2024-11-05` and `2025-03-26` clients, a client with no `elicitation` capability, and one that offers URL mode only. A `2024-11-05` client sees the router exactly as before. A capable client is never given a token: the model cannot answer for you, and a `confirm` it sends is ignored.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Ask a human：Anything but an explicit yes runs nothing and returns `USER_DECLINED <outcome>`: `decline`, `cancel`, `unconfirmed` (accepted without ticking confirm), `error` (the client answered with a JSON-RPC error) or `timeout`. If the client closes the connection while the dialog is open, nothing runs and the router exits. Each question is written to the call log as a `kind: "policy"` row with `"via": "elicitation"` and the `outcome` (`accept` or the reason it did not run).
dsh-tool-guardian README · Ask a human：`TOOL_GUARDIAN_ELICIT_TIMEOUT` is how many seconds to wait for your answer (default 300); a reply that arrives later is ignored.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Ask a human：**Claude Code** shows the dialog only in interactive terminal sessions. A non-interactive session (`claude -p`, CI) cannot show it and cancels, which the model sees as `USER_DECLINED cancel`: there, use `deny`, or accept that the call will not run. This is tested against a scripted client that speaks each of the protocol revisions above; it has not yet been run against a live Claude Code session.

The hook is tested against Claude Code's documented `PreToolUse` payload and against a payload captured from a live Claude Code 2.1.296 session, where deny mode blocked the call (see [Works with](#works-with)); [`examples/claude-code/settings.json`](examples/claude-code/settings.json) is the same block. dsh-tool-guardian README · Hook rules file：```bash
tool-guardian --hook-pretooluse --rules ~/.tool-guardian/hook-rules.json
```

```json
{"deny":  [{"tool": "Bash", "args": {"command": "\\brm\\s+-rf\\b"}, "reason": "no recursive deletes"},
           {"tool": "WebFetch"}],
 "allow": [{"tool": "Bash", "args": {"command": "^git (status|log|diff)"}}]}
```

dsh-tool-guardian README · Hook rules file：Rules run before the default behaviour. `tool` is a regex matched against the whole tool name; each `args` key is a
regex searched in that `tool_input` field; every listed key must match. Deny rules are checked first and win: the
call is blocked with `reason` (or a default naming the rule). An allow match skips tool-guardian's own check and lets
the call go on to Claude Code's normal permission flow; it approves nothing. No match, no file, or an unreadable file:
the default behaviour, unchanged. The hook only sees the tools its `matcher` sends it, so widen the matcher (e.g.
`Bash|PowerShell|WebFetch`) for rules on other tools.

dsh-tool-guardian README · Design notes (the parts that matter)：- **Failure is loud, on purpose.** A router is a single point of failure: without one a broken server costs you that server; behind one it could cost you all of them. So an unreachable backend is reported as `UNKNOWN` with its real error, **never as an empty tool list**. A model that asks for a server and gets `[]` concludes the capability doesn't exist and quietly works around it — the exact failure this avoids.
- **Built for models, not just machines.** It accepts a tool's `args` as either an object or a JSON string, aliases the near-misses models actually send (`query`/`name` → `server`), and ends every result with the concrete **NEXT STEP** to call — because a model that receives a catalogue and no instruction tends to stop there instead of finishing the task.
- **The catalogue names your servers.** Six unnamed generic tools give a model no reason to believe any capability exists, so it improvises. Naming the servers in the tool description costs a few tokens and is the difference between a catalogue the model opens and six tools it ignores.

dsh-tool-guardian README · The guardian family：One of four free, MIT-licensed guardians for people running local models, each answering one question from the outside: tool-guardian (what do my tools cost the window?), context-guardian (will this session hit the limit?), stack-guardian (is my stack healthy?), code-guardian (is this code safe to run?).

dsh-tool-guardian README · What it does *not* do (yet)：- It does not merge or rename tools; it proxies them faithfully. `call_tool(server, tool, args)` reaches the real tool unchanged.
- Over plain MCP it cannot see a client's shell calls; see [bypass detection and its limits](#bypass-detection-over-plain-mcp-and-its-limits).
- **The router's own tools cost about 1,100 tokens** of `tools/list` (with no backends; more with a long server list). With one small server behind it, that is close to break-even; it pays off from a few servers up. `TOOL_GUARDIAN_TERSE=1` (or `TOOL_GUARDIAN_PRESET=small`) brings it to ~620 tokens.
- The token figures are an estimate (characters ÷ 3.5) unless `tiktoken` is installed; `--usage` always uses the estimate.
- `--usage` counts what the router did, not what the model would have done without it: the "avoided" figure assumes every session would otherwise have loaded the full catalogue, and it cannot tell a model that skipped the router from one that had nothing to call (see `--bypass-summary`).
- It has no card in the DSH web UI; configure it in `~/.dsh/settings.yaml` ([docs/dsh-settings.md](docs/dsh-settings.md)).
